title: hosted-api-developer-journey-hooks-and-pricing-hypotheses
content:
Purpose:
This is a working brief with compact messaging hooks, competitive notes, and pricing phrasing experiments for the Hosted API positioning aimed strictly at engineering-first buyers.

Context / goal:
- Audience: backend/frontend engineers, ML engineers, platform teams evaluating APIs for production LLM features.
- Primary job-to-be-done: get from signup -> authenticated first call -> measurable delta (latency/cost comparison or prototype) within a half-day.
- Secondary: create pricing language that reduces friction for trials and clearly separates hosted pay-as-you-go vs. reserved/dedicated.

Topline developer value props (short statements to test across pages/emails):
- "Start in minutes, ship with production SLAs: predictable latency, token controls, and rollbackable model pins."
- "Same API from demo to dedicated GPU pools—no refactor when you scale."
- "Transparent cost and performance: token + latency breakdowns so engineers can tune, not guess."

Primary developer personas (brief):
- Prototype-first engineer: wants quick POC, low friction, cares about sample latency and simple SDKs.
- Product/feature engineer: expects stability, observability, and minimal changes between dev and prod.
- Platform engineer: cares about billing predictability, VPC/private options, and rollout/rollback primitives.

Quickstart angles (3 distinct hooks to A/B test):
1) "Hello, 5 Requests" (fastest path):
   - Goal: first meaningful response in under 5 requests/calls.
   - Steps: Signup -> Get key -> 1-line curl example -> call + streaming response -> sample JSON for logs.
   - Landing page microcopy: "Call the API, get structured text back, integrate in <10 minutes."
   - Success metric: time-to-first-call (target < 10 min), % users completing code snippet.

2) "Replace your current LLM in 20 minutes" (migration empathy):
   - Goal: show parity/upgrade path from competitor API.
   - Steps: quick mapping table (endpoint/naming), code diff snippet for request/response compatibility, auto-fallback example to cheaper variant.
   - Microcopy: "Keep your code, swap the endpoint—improve latency and lower cost per token."
   - Success metric: sign-ups mentioning competitor names in form, demo requests.

3) "From PoC to SLA (demo-to-prod)" (ops-forward):
   - Goal: highlight observability and rollout features.
   - Steps: create route, enable tracing, demo canary rollout to 5% -> automatic fallback to cheaper model on error.
   - Microcopy: "Ship with confidence—canary, metrics, and automatic fallbacks included."
   - Success metric: clicks to 'enable rollouts', time to create route.

Pricing-language drafts (short experiments to test):
- Option A (developer-friendly, explicit):
  "Free tier: 20k tokens/month for experiments. Pay-as-you-go: $0.0007 per token for generation tokens, $0.0003 per token for embeddings. Reserved instances and Dedicated capacity available for predictable workloads."
  Microcopy variant: "Start free, pay for what you send. Upgrade to Dedicated for SLA-backed performance."

- Option B (tiered simplicity):
  "Starter (Free): 20k tokens + community support. Scale (PayGo): token pricing, per-request rate limits adjustable. Business: reserved credits and discounted token rates, enterprise support and SSO."
  Microcopy variant: "Pick the plan that matches how you run: trial, scale, or enterprise."

- Option C (engineering-first framing):
  "Transparent unit pricing: per-token + per-request latency surcharge. Use our cost estimator to see exact spend for your sample traces. Reserved capacity available for monthly commitments with X% discount and a latency SLO."
  Microcopy variant: "Know the cost of every token—estimate, simulate, then commit."

Pricing microcopy notes (tone experiments):
- Technical tone: include concrete token numbers, examples (e.g., 1k tokens ~= 300 words).
- Business-friendly tone: emphasize free trial and predictable monthly invoices.
- Ops tone: call out SLOs, dedicated pools, and audit logs.

Competitive differentiators to emphasize (short bullets for page/one-pager):
- Unified runtime: same API and SDKs across hosted, dedicated, private deployments—low engineering lift when moving to prod.
- Latency transparency: published perf profiles per model + sample p95/p99 across regions.
- Operational features: canary rollouts, fallback routing, KV cache, and tracing hooks out-of-the-box.
- Cost tools: estimator, batching suggestions, and quantization recommendations tied to actual workload.

Risks & rebuttals (customer objections and quick counters):
- "We host ourselves to save money." -> "Total cost of ownership includes engineering + storage + ops. We provide quantifiable per-token cost and migration playbooks to measure real savings in weeks."
- "Vendor lock-in" -> "Open models supported, model catalog transparent, you can pin versions; SDKs are tiny wrappers over REST."

Experiments & measurement plan (next 6 weeks):
- Launch A/B landing pages for the 3 quickstarts; measure: time-to-first-call, sample-run completions, sign-up->billing conversion rate.
- Pricing language test: run two pricing banners (Tech-heavy vs Tiered) on focused traffic; track click-throughs to pricing docs and trial-to-paid conversion.
- Onboarding flow tweak: add a prefilled cURL with user's language choice; measure snippet usage and drop-off.

Copy snippets for CTA testing (short):
- "Get your first response in 5 minutes" / "Start free, no card required" / "Estimate your monthly cost"

Open questions and TODOs:
- PR to engineering required to expose real-time p99 telemetry for landing page examples (see CONFLUENCE-ENG-8472).
- Need security-approved phrasing for "SLA-backed" in marketing; legal review required.
- Design: 3 micro-illustrations for the quickstart funnels (proto, migrate, scale).

Slack notes / links for follow-up:
- #growth -> ask for 2 hero emails to test developer tone.
- #product -> confirm rollout UI copy and flag required telemetry events.
- Jira: JIRA-GTM-312 tracks the landing page implementation.

Bottom line (one-sentence):
Position Hosted API as "the engineer's quickest path from prototype to production-grade inference"—emphasize speed of first call, predictable unit economics, and operational controls that lower long-term engineering costs.
